stances.claim: The Yale scholarship that never materialized became, in retrospect, one of the most formative disappointments of Art's life -- he had wanted it badly, not for prestige but for completion; he sensed even then that law was not merely a profession but a calling that demanded the sharpest tools available.

stances.claim: It was at this juncture that Jovito R. Salonga stepped fully into his life -- not merely as a former dean, but as a moral architect. Salonga had walked the path Art dreamed of -- UP, Harvard, Yale -- having absorbed not only legal technique but the ethical traditions of Western jurisprudence; when Yale became unreachable for his young protégé, Salonga made a quiet offer that would change everything: 'If you cannot go to Yale, Yale will come to you.'
stances.rhetorical_move: moral-architect-not-merely-dean role-reframe + UP-Harvard-Yale credential-triad + quiet-offer-that-would-change-everything + Yale-will-come-to-you titular-quoted aphorism

stances.claim: At Salonga, Ordoñez and Associates, where Art apprenticed from 1961 to 1963, law was not practiced as transaction -- it was practiced as responsibility; cases were dissected for principle as much as outcome; victory without integrity was considered failure; political expediency was distrusted; conscience mattered.
stances.rhetorical_move: law-as-responsibility-not-transaction firm-culture + principle-as-much-as-outcome value + victory-without-integrity-is-failure + conscience-mattered ethics-roster

stances.claim: Here Art learned something more valuable than advanced degrees: judgment. Salonga introduced him to a lineage of Filipino legal giants -- Jose W. Diokno, whose human rights advocacy would become legend; Claudio O. Teehankee, whose judicial courage would later define an era. These were not men who merely interpreted law. They embodied it.
stances.rhetorical_move: judgment-more-valuable-than-degrees thesis + Filipino-legal-giants-lineage Diokno-Teehankee tandem + embodied-not-merely-interpreted titular distinction

stances.claim: Art absorbed their example with reverence -- he learned that law divorced from morality becomes tyranny by another name, that judges must sometimes stand alone and accept isolation as the cost of fidelity; this apprenticeship forged his moral spine.

one_paragraph_summary: Art's mentorship chapter, reframing the Yale denial as 'one of the most formative disappointments' that redirected him into Salonga's orbit. Jovito R. Salonga -- UP, Harvard, Yale-credentialed and 'a figure of moral and intellectual authority' -- steps into Art's life 'not merely as a former dean, but as a moral architect,' offering the chapter's titular aphorism: 'If you cannot go to Yale, Yale will come to you.' Apprenticing at Salonga, Ordoñez and Associates (1961-1963), Art encounters a firm culture where 'law was not practiced as transaction -- it was practiced as responsibility,' where 'victory without integrity was considered failure,' and where conscience mattered more than expediency. Salonga introduces him to the Filipino-legal-giants lineage -- Jose W. Diokno ('human rights advocacy would become legend') and Claudio O. Teehankee ('judicial courage would later define an era') -- men who 'were not... merely interpreting law; they embodied it.' From them Art learns that 'law divorced from morality becomes tyranny by another name' and that 'judges must sometimes stand alone and accept isolation as the cost of fidelity.' This apprenticeship 'forged his moral spine.' When he leaves in 1963 to establish his own firm, PABLAW, he carries not only legal competence but a philosophy: 'success must never outpace conscience.'
